overview: Plan Fort Lauderdale around its Atlantic beach, New River, Intracoastal Waterway, arts districts, and canal-side neighborhoods.
The water network is not background scenery—it is the organizing geography of the city.

highlights.description: Use the destination's defining landscapes, neighborhoods, and cultural sites to structure the visit.

thingsToDo.title: Fort Lauderdale Beach
thingsToDo.description: Walk or bike the beachfront promenade and use the Atlantic shoreline for an early swim or sunrise before the midday heat.

thingsToDo.title: Las Olas Boulevard
thingsToDo.description: Follow Las Olas from downtown toward the beach for restaurants, galleries, shops, and canal-side city scenery.

thingsToDo.title: Riverwalk and the New River
thingsToDo.description: Use the riverfront path to connect parks, cultural sites, historic buildings, and boat traffic through downtown.

thingsToDo.title: Bonnet House Museum & Gardens
thingsToDo.description: Visit the historic estate near the beach for art, architecture, gardens, and a surviving pocket of older coastal Fort Lauderdale.

thingsToDo.title: Hugh Taylor Birch State Park
thingsToDo.description: Explore the state park between the Intracoastal and Atlantic for shade, trails, paddling, and a natural contrast to the developed beachfront.

thingsToDo.title: Intracoastal Waterway cruise
thingsToDo.description: See the city's canals, marinas, bridges, and waterfront neighborhoods from the water for the clearest geographic overview.

bestTimeToVisit.title: Cooler months are easiest for outdoor planning
bullets: Late fall through early spring generally brings lower humidity and comfortable outdoor conditions.
Summer is hot, humid, and storm-prone; start exposed activities early and keep afternoon plans flexible.
Busy winter and holiday periods reward advance reservations for popular tours and timed attractions.

travelTips: Group each day by geography instead of crossing the region repeatedly.
Use early mornings for exposed outdoor activities and waterfront time.
Check park, marine, and weather conditions before nature-focused plans.
Treat nearby municipalities and protected areas as separate destinations with their own access rules.

faq.q: How many days should I plan for Fort Lauderdale?
faq.a: Two to three days is a good starting point for the core sights plus one outdoor or regional experience.

faq.q: Is Fort Lauderdale good for outdoor travelers?
faq.a: Yes. The strongest itineraries combine the destination itself with nearby water, parks, preserves, or trails.
It depends on the destination, but a car or guided tour is often useful for protected lands and regional excursions.

faq.q: Should I book tours in advance?
faq.a: For high-demand wildlife, boating, park, and holiday-period experiences, advance booking is sensible.

sections.heading: Overview
paragraphs: Fort Lauderdale is an incorporated Broward County city where coastal tourism meets a dense waterway system and growing downtown.

sections.heading: Geography & setting
paragraphs: The New River, canals, and Intracoastal Waterway connect inland neighborhoods to the Atlantic.

sections.heading: History & culture
paragraphs: Las Olas, downtown, Flagler Village, and the beach district offer distinct arts, dining, and nightlife experiences.

sections.heading: Outdoor & seasonal highlights
paragraphs: Beach time, boating, paddling, and Hugh Taylor Birch State Park are central outdoor experiences.

sections.heading: Getting around
paragraphs: Group the beach and Bonnet House together; handle downtown, Las Olas, and Riverwalk as another compact cluster.
